tldr: State-of-the-art coding agents with trial-and-error access to a simulator can autonomously synthesize generalized execution programs that outperform traditional TAMP planners, all without hand-crafted abstractions or domain definitions.
hero_caption: Overview of this study. Coding agents write generalized Python programs (policies) while interacting with a simulator inside a sandbox. Compared to hand-engineered TAMP planners, they maintain high success rates even as object counts grow, while requiring orders of magnitude less inference compute time.
overview:
Task and motion planning (TAMP) solves discrete action selection and continuous motion planning together. It is an inherently difficult robotics problem because long search horizons are tightly coupled with geometric, kinematic, and dynamic constraints. Generalized TAMP tries to tackle this by leveraging regularities across problem instances to reduce planning effort. However, existing methods still rely on heavy manual modeling and symbolic definitions by human experts.

In this paper, the authors asked a simple question: What if we give modern coding agents just a task description and simulator access, letting them experiment autonomously to synthesize control programs that generalize to unseen instances? Within a fixed budget, each agent runs its own test scripts and modifies its program while observing simulator behavior. The finalized program is then frozen and evaluated at test time without querying any LLMs.

The authors evaluated Claude Code (Opus 5) and Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra) on 28 simulated environments, including the KinDER benchmark and PDDLStream domains. Across 980 synthesized programs, they conducted a large-scale evaluation totaling 98,000 episodes on held-out test instances.

Programs synthesized by coding agents achieved mean success rates of 56% to 95%, well outperforming carefully hand-engineered TAMP planners (47% mean success). Their performance held up remarkably well as object counts grew, and execution-time computation dropped by over an order of magnitude. These results show that autonomous coding agents are a strong baseline for generalized TAMP.
contributions: Systematically demonstrating that coding agents, through simulator interaction, can synthesize generalized programs to solve TAMP problems without manual engineering.
Establishing a large-scale, rigorous evaluation protocol covering 28 environments, 980 programs, and 98,000 episodes, comparing agents against hand-engineered planners and static LLM baselines.
Observing advanced physical reasoning behaviors, such as agents writing test suites to actively explore edge cases, calibrating robot kinematic errors, and building custom inverse kinematics solvers.
Showing that agents can autonomously discover unexpected, highly efficient strategies that utilize non-prehensile manipulation or environment layouts, unseen in hand-engineered planners.

sections.heading: Can coding agents replace the craftsmanship of TAMP?
sections.summary: TAMP is inherently difficult due to tightly coupled geometric and physical constraints. This study tests whether modern coding agents, interacting with a simulator, can synthesize generalized control programs across 28 environments without hand-crafted abstractions.
sections.details:
Task and motion planning (TAMP) remains a fundamentally hard computational problem, even with full observability and object-centric states. That is because discrete choices (like which object to pick) are tightly coupled with continuous geometric and kinematic constraints (such as reachability and collision avoidance). Generalized TAMP aims to address this difficulty by leveraging regularities across problem instances to speed up planning. However, it typically requires human experts to manually craft predicates, samplers, and skills.

Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable strides in code generation. Yet prior work showed that giving LLMs geometric state information in prompts often fails for physical decision-making like TAMP. To bridge this gap, the authors propose AgenticGenPlan: letting modern coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) actively probe a simulator and synthesize programs through test-driven development.

In a large-scale evaluation across 28 simulation environments, 7 synthesis methods, and 5 runs each (980 generated programs tested on 100 unseen instances, for 98,000 episodes total), agents clearly came out ahead. On the 16 environments with an official planner, the agents reached 56% to 95% mean success, compared to 47% for hand-engineered planners. Even when object counts scaled up and caused planners to time out, the agents' programs maintained high success rates with very little computation time.

captions.F2: Surprising successful strategies discovered autonomously by agents. Examples include re-orienting a tool to scoop up many balls at once (third row from top) or ignoring a designated sweeping tool and using the robot arm itself to sweep blocks out (fifth row from top)—creative solutions not found in the original papers.

sections.heading: Problem setting: Program synthesis with simulator access and evaluation on unseen instances
sections.summary: The benchmark uses finite-horizon goal-directed MDPs with fully observable, object-centric states. Agents freely interact with the simulator during development to synthesize a Python program, which then solves unseen instances at test time without an LLM.
sections.details:
### II-A MDPs and Simulator Access
The problem is formulated as a finite-horizon goal-directed Markov Decision Process (MDP: $\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,R,\rho,H\rangle$). The state $\mathcal{S}$ is fully observable and object-centric, containing poses, geometries, joint angles, and velocities for each object. Problem instances are sampled from the initial state distribution $\rho$, with varying object counts and layouts. The agent is given access to the simulator's `reset` and `step` APIs.

### II-B TAMP Environments
The TAMP environments studied here focus strictly on physical reasoning, removing perception and language ambiguities. They feature long horizons, sparse rewards, and narrow reachable action spaces that depend heavily on discrete tool and sub-goal choices.

### II-C Synthesis and Evaluation
During synthesis, the agent receives a task description, simulator access, and a fixed API budget. The agent's final deliverable is a policy program $a_t = \pi(h_t)$ that outputs actions given history.
During evaluation, this synthesized program is completely frozen. No LLM queries occur. The program is evaluated on held-out initial states $s_0 \sim \rho$ not seen during synthesis. Metrics include goal success rate within a per-instance time budget $\tau$ (60 seconds) and computation time per action.

sections.heading: Agent mechanisms and baselines: Interactive development in a sandbox
sections.summary: Claude Code (Opus 5) and Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol / GPT-6 Astra) operate inside isolated containers. Baselines include hand-engineered TAMP planners, a non-interactive LLM method (LLMGenPlan), and one-shot generation.
sections.details:
### III-A Coding Agents
The authors used Claude Code (Opus 5) and Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra) as agent backends. Agents run in network-isolated Docker sandboxes. Third-party libraries are restricted to NumPy and SciPy to prevent reliance on existing TAMP solvers.

Agents receive only a task description and a client class to call the simulator. They get no environment source code and no hand-crafted planning predicates or skills (the main setting). Agents write Python scripts, run the simulator, observe outcomes, and implement a policy class with `reset` and `get_action` methods. Every edit is committed to a local Git repository to track development. For comparison, the authors also tested a "+ source" setting where agents can read the environment source code and internal helper functions (such as inverse kinematics).

### III-B Baselines
The following baselines were evaluated for comparison:
- **TAMP Planner**: The official benchmark implementations combining symbolic search, continuous samplers, and hand-crafted motion planning skills.
- **LLMGenPlan**: A non-agentic LLM generalized planning baseline from prior work. It has no terminal access; instead, the LLM reads environment source code and refines its program through fixed error-log feedback loops.
- **One-shot**: A baseline evaluating the very first program output by LLMGenPlan without iterative refinement.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Outperforming hand-engineered planners with surprising autonomous strategies
sections.summary: Across 28 environments, Codex (GPT-6 Astra) and Claude Code (Opus 5) clearly outperformed hand-engineered planners and other LLM baselines. Agents built custom test suites to catch edge cases and calibrated robot kinematic models on their own.
sections.details:
### IV-A Environment Setup
Experiments used 25 environments from the KinDER benchmark (Kinematic2D/3D and Dynamic2D/3D) plus 3 PDDLStream domains. Each method underwent 5 independent synthesis runs with a $20 API budget per run. Programs were evaluated on 100 random seeds never seen during synthesis.

### IV-B Results and Analysis
Key findings include:
- **Comparison with Hand-Engineered Planners**: On the 16 environments with available planners (47% mean planner success), Sol reached 56%, Opus reached 82%, and Astra reached 95%. Astra outperformed the planner on 15 out of 16 environments.
- **Autonomous Edge-Case Testing**: Agents wrote their own test scripts to uncover failure modes. For example, in StickButton, an agent's script systematically collected cases where the stick was too close to a wall to grasp or where buttons were high up. It then synthesized a multi-step strategy: grasp the stick sideways to pull it away from the wall, re-grasp it from below, and press the button.
- **Internal Model Calibration**: In Shelf, end-effector poses are not directly observed. Opus wrote an initial arm kinematic model from scratch, ran experiments picking and moving a cube, and reduced its end-effector position error (RMSE) from 38.9 mm down to 1.8 mm, building a working custom inverse kinematics (IK) solver.
- **Computational Efficiency**: Test-time inference was fast. While planners averaged 29 seconds per instance, Opus programs averaged 2.1 seconds, and Astra programs averaged 0.5 seconds. At the action level, Astra produced concise closed-form control logic running in just 1.3 ms per step.
- **Impact of Source Code Access**: Giving agents source code ("+ source") boosted success even further (74% to 84% for Opus, 86% to 95% for Astra). However, LLMGenPlan with the exact same source code managed only 28%. This highlights that interactive, agentic testing and refinement are the decisive factors.

captions.F3: Agent testing and physical system identification. Left (StickButton): The agent's self-written test found that sticks near walls cannot be grasped from below, leading to a multi-step pull-and-re-grasp strategy. Right (Shelf): The agent moves the arm, measures end-effector and block positions, and calibrates its internal kinematic model to solve inverse kinematics (IK).
captions.F4: Strategy refinement during synthesis (Sol log on the Blocked environment). The initial approach (A) scored 15% success due to foreground obstacles. After commit (B) added a fallback to retrieve spare blocks from a distant table, success jumped to 56%.

sections.heading: Related work: Lineage of TAMP learning, foundation models, and coding agents
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes itself within generalized TAMP, LLM-guided planning, and robotic code synthesis. It stands out by having general-purpose agents write policies from scratch without relying on specific TAMP frameworks.
sections.details:
### V-A Generalized Planning and Learning for TAMP
TAMP research has produced frameworks like PDDLStream that connect symbolic search to continuous sampling. Generalized TAMP has explored learning samplers and search heuristics across instances, but these still require domain-specific representations tailored to each framework.

### V-B Foundation Models for Task and Motion Planning
Prior works integrating LLMs into TAMP use them as high-level task plan guides or have them output constraint-specification programs (like PRoC3S or MOPS). In contrast, this work does not assume existing TAMP abstraction layers; agents freely implement search, sampling, and optimization algorithms directly in code.

### V-C Agentic Synthesis of Robotic Programs
Following Code-as-Policies, many works have used LLMs to write robotic control code, with agents like RHO and ASPIRE using execution feedback to refine skills. However, these focus largely on standard manipulation benchmarks rather than the intricate geometric and dynamic constraints of TAMP.

### V-D Systematic Evaluation of Embodied Agents
Many prior evaluations keep LLMs in the control loop during task execution. In contrast, this work uses simulator interaction only during synthesis to iteratively refine code, leaving a standalone, frozen program that runs at high speed during testing without LLM calls.

sections.heading: Limitations and outlook: The potential of autonomous physical reasoning for next-generation planning
sections.summary: While limited by full observability assumptions and potential training data overlap, the agents' trial-and-error logs and creative strategies demonstrate genuine reasoning. Coding agents represent a strong baseline for future TAMP research.
sections.details:
### Limitations
The current setup assumes fully observable, object-centric states and unlimited simulator calls during the synthesis phase. Its applicability to real-world conditions with perceptual uncertainty and partial observability is not yet proven. In addition, one cannot completely rule out that frontier model pre-training data contained parts of the benchmark code. However, raw agent logs showing parameter tuning against the simulator, alongside novel non-prehensile and avoidance behaviors not present in the literature, provide strong evidence of active physical reasoning rather than mere memorization.

### Conclusions
General-purpose coding agents can understand environment physics through simulator interaction and generate generalized programs that outperform hand-engineered classical planners—without any human-crafted abstractions or domain definitions. These results show that coding agents are an essential, strong baseline for future TAMP research.

takeaways: Given simulator APIs and the freedom to do test-driven development, coding agents synthesize generalized programs that outperform hand-engineered classical TAMP planners.
At test time, the synthesized Python programs run on their own without LLM queries, achieving millisecond-to-second inference speeds.
Agents do not merely write code; they run scripts to collect edge cases and calibrate kinematic errors to solve IK, autonomously carrying out complex engineering workflows.
For problems where non-interactive LLM baselines (LLMGenPlan) fail, giving the model tool execution and simulator interaction leads to dramatic performance gains.
limitations: The approach assumes fully observable, object-centric states; robustness against real-world perception noise and camera-based state estimation remains untested.
Success rates remain low in 3D dynamic environments (Dynamic3D) involving complex contact physics, such as scooping or pouring gravel and large sets of small objects.
Because training data for proprietary frontier models is not public, it is difficult to completely determine how much benchmark code or related material was seen during pre-training.
